items.title: Holding a quarterly review
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: A quarterly review is a short, regular meeting to check results against the plan and decide what to keep, change or stop. Gather the numbers beforehand: sales, margin, cash, and the progress of each goal. Spend the meeting on the differences between plan and result, ask why, and avoid reading out figures everyone has seen. End with decisions: a named owner and a date for each. Keep a one-page record, and carry unfinished items forward only if they still matter. Doing it every quarter, at a fixed time, catches problems while there is still room to act and makes the annual plan a living document.

items.title: Mission and vision
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: A mission says why the organisation exists and who it serves today; a vision says what it hopes to become. Values describe how people behave on the way. A useful mission is short, plain and specific enough to say no to something; a vision is a picture of the future that people can work towards. Write them with the team, not for them. Use them in decisions: does this fit our mission? Does it move us towards our vision? Repeat them until people can say them from memory. A mission statement on a wall that nobody uses is only decoration.

items.title: Finding your ideal customer
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Your ideal customer is the type of person or business you serve best and who gets the most value from what you do. Describe them specifically: who they are, what problem they have, what they do today to solve it, how they decide to buy, what they can afford and where you can reach them. Start from your best existing customers: what do they have in common? Talk to them. Choose a small group to serve first rather than everyone, since a clear focus makes your message sharper and your marketing cheaper. Test whether you could find ten of them this week. Revisit your description as you learn.

items.title: Franchising and licensing
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Franchising lets others run a business under your brand and system in return for fees; licensing lets others use your brand, product or rights for a fee. Both can grow a business using other people's money and effort, but both need a proven, written system that others can copy, clear contracts, training and support. You give up some control, and franchisees' conduct affects your brand. Agree fees, territory, standards, what happens if they fail and how the agreement ends. Check the rules for your country, which may include disclosure duties. Take advice from a lawyer who knows franchising.
